title: Even Moses and Samuel Could Not Save Them
summary: God tells Jeremiah that even the great intercessors Moses and Samuel could not turn him from judging Judah, and he names the sword, famine, and captivity that are coming because of the sins that reach back to King Manasseh. Jeremiah then cries out in his second confession, cursing the day his mother bore him, recalling the joy he once found in God's words, and accusing God of being like a stream that runs dry. God answers with a call to return and a renewed promise to make him a wall of bronze.
story: Chapter 14 ended with the people's prayer, and chapter 15 gives God's answer: no. Where chapter 14 described the drought, chapter 15 widens to the full catalogue of judgment, and then, as in chapters 11 and 12, the focus turns from the nation to the prophet. The pressure of carrying this message has isolated Jeremiah from everyone, and he lets God hear exactly how much it hurts. God's reply does not remove the burden; it recommissions him. The promise of verse 20 repeats almost word for word what God said at Jeremiah's call (1:18-19), so the chapter brings the prophet back to the beginning, with far more understanding of what that first promise would cost.
historical:
Verse 4 lays the blame for the coming disaster on "what Manasseh son of Hezekiah king of Judah did in Jerusalem". Manasseh reigned for about fifty-five years in the first half of the seventh century BC (2 Kings 21:1), the longest reign of any king of Judah, during which Judah was a vassal of Assyria. The book of Kings charges him with rebuilding the high places, setting up altars to Baal and to the stars in the temple courts, sacrificing his own son, practicing sorcery, and filling Jerusalem with innocent blood (2 Kings 21:2-16). Kings says that even Josiah's reform did not turn away the LORD's anger over Manasseh (2 Kings 23:26-27; 24:3-4). Jeremiah shares this view: the generations had built up a debt that a few good years did not erase. Chronicles adds that Manasseh later humbled himself and repented (2 Chronicles 33:10-16), a detail Kings does not mention.

The "iron from the north" in verse 12 again points to Babylon, the power no one in Judah could break. The judgments listed in verses 2 and 3 (death, sword, famine, captivity, and bodies left for dogs and birds) describe what siege and conquest meant in the ancient world, and they came true in the Babylonian campaigns of 597 and 588 to 586 BC.
cultural:
Moses and Samuel were remembered as Israel's great intercessors. Moses stood between the people and God's anger after the golden calf (Exodus 32:11-14, 30-32), and Samuel prayed for Israel at Mizpah and promised never to stop praying for them (1 Samuel 7:5-9; 12:23). To say that even they could not change God's mind was the strongest possible way to say that the time for intercession had passed.

In verse 10, Jeremiah says he has "neither lent nor borrowed". Lending and borrowing were notorious sources of quarrels and curses in the ancient world, since debtors resented creditors and creditors hounded debtors. Jeremiah's point is that he has given no one ordinary cause for hatred, yet everyone curses him. The "band of revelers" in verse 17 translates a word for a circle of friends gathered in intimate conversation, the ordinary social life of a town. Jeremiah was cut off from it. The image in verse 18 comes from the dry streambeds (wadis) of the region, which run with water in the rainy season but vanish in summer, so that a traveler counting on them finds nothing.
literary: The chapter has two halves. Verses 1 to 9 are God's speech of judgment, full of grim lists and rhetorical questions ("Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem?"), ending with a mother of seven sons whose sun sets at noon, a reversal of Hannah's song in which the barren woman bears seven (1 Samuel 2:5). Verses 10 to 21 are the second of Jeremiah's confessions, a dialogue in which the prophet complains (verse 10), God replies (verses 11 to 14, a passage whose Hebrew is difficult and whose connection to the context is debated; verses 13 and 14 closely resemble 17:3-4), Jeremiah complains again (verses 15 to 18), and God answers (verses 19 to 21). The key verb shuv, to turn or return, is used several times in verse 19 in a play on words: if Jeremiah returns, God will restore him; the people must turn to him, but he must not turn to them.

outline.t: Not even Moses and Samuel: four destroyers
Jerusalem forsaken: widows and the mother of seven
Jeremiah's woe and God's first reply
Your words were my joy, yet you are like a mirage
If you return: a fortified wall of bronze

doctrines.note: Jeremiah's pain is caused by his faithfulness, not his sin, and he speaks of it without pretense. God does not rebuke him for grieving; he calls him away from bitterness back to his post.

Remarkably, the call to return in verse 19 is addressed to the prophet himself. Even God's faithful servant can drift into accusation and need to turn back, and God meets that turning with restoration.
"Your words were found, and I ate them" pictures God's word as food taken in and made part of the self. The same word that gave Jeremiah joy also set him apart and brought him into conflict.

words.note: Akhzav, deceptive or failing, used for a stream that dries up. In verse 18 Jeremiah uses it against God: "You have indeed become like a mirage to me". It is one of the boldest accusations anywhere in Scripture, and the irony is strong, since in 2:13 God called himself "the fountain of living water". The prophet feels that the fountain has failed him.

Shuv, to turn, return, or repent, one of the most important verbs in Jeremiah. In verse 19 God plays on its range: if you return (in repentance), I will restore you (bring you back to your place); they must turn to you, but you must not turn to them. Repentance in the Old Testament is a change of direction, not only a change of feeling.

Cherpah, reproach, scorn, or disgrace. Jeremiah says, "I endure reproach for Your honor" (verse 15). His suffering is not random; he is mocked because he carries God's name. The word often describes the insult a people suffers when their God seems unable to help them.

christ: Moses and Samuel stood in the gap for Israel but could not avert this judgment. The New Testament presents Jesus as the intercessor whose prayer does not fail, because he has not only pleaded for his people but also borne their judgment himself (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). That is a contrast drawn from the whole story rather than a prediction in this chapter. Jeremiah's experience also anticipates Jesus in several ways: he is a man of strife, cursed though he has wronged no one, sitting alone under God's hand, bearing reproach for God's sake. Paul applies similar language to Christ, who bore the insults of those who insulted God (Romans 15:3, quoting Psalm 69:9). The image of eating God's words recurs in Ezekiel 3:1-3 and Revelation 10:9-10, and Jesus himself said that man lives by every word from God's mouth (Matthew 4:4).

hard.q: Is it wrong for Jeremiah to call God a mirage, and why does God tell him to repent?
hard.a: Jeremiah's complaint is shocking, and the Bible keeps it. Faithful people in Scripture regularly speak to God with this kind of honesty (Psalm 88, Job, Habakkuk), and God does not treat lament as rebellion. At the same time, God's reply in verse 19 does call Jeremiah to turn back, and to speak what is precious rather than worthless. Interpreters differ on what exactly needed correcting. Some think it was the accusation that God is untrustworthy; others think it was the self-pity and the desire for revenge in verse 15; others see a prophet close to giving up his calling. What is clear is that God's rebuke comes with restoration, not rejection: if you return, I will restore you, and I am with you. The chapter holds together two things readers often separate: the freedom to bring any complaint to God and the need to let God answer it.

questions: Jeremiah remembered when God's words were his joy. What has fed your faith in the past, and what has happened to that joy?
Jeremiah says he sat alone because God's hand was on him. When has faithfulness cost you belonging, and how did you carry it?
God calls even his prophet to return. Where might you need to turn back, not from open sin, but from bitterness or discouragement?
